pr_title: M-map full chunks of Head from disk
pr_body:
tl-dr desc for the PR from @krasi-georgiev 

-----------------
When appending to the head and a chunk is full it is flushed to the disk and m-mapped (memory mapped) to free up memory

Prom startup now happens in these stages
 - Iterate the m-maped chunks from disk and keep a map of series reference to its slice of mmapped chunks.
- Iterate the WAL as usual. Whenever we create a new series, look for it's mmapped chunks in the map created before and add it to that series.


If a head chunk is corrupted the currpted one and all chunks after that are deleted and the data after the corruption is recovered from the existing WAL which means that a corruption in m-mapped files results in NO data loss.


[Mmaped chunks format](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/master/tsdb/docs/format/head_chunks.md)  - main difference is that the chunk for mmaping now also includes series reference because there is no index for mapping series to chunks.
[The block chunks](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/master/tsdb/docs/format/chunks.md) are accessed from the index which includes the offsets for the chunks in the chunks file - example - chunks of series ID have offsets 200, 500 etc in the chunk files.
In case of mmaped chunks, the offsets are stored in memory and accessed from that. During WAL replay, these offsets are restored by iterating all m-mapped chunks as stated above by matching the series id present in the chunk header and offset of that chunk in that file.

**Prombench results**

_WAL Replay_

1h Wal reply time
30% less wal reply time - 4m31 vs 3m36
2h Wal reply time
20% less wal reply time - 8m16 vs 7m

_Memory During WAL Replay_

[High Churn](http://prombench.prometheus.io/grafana/d/7gmLoNDmz/prombench?orgId=1&var-RuleGroup=All&var-pr-number=6679&from=1588177559275&to=1588182978872)	
10-15% less RAM -  32gb vs 28gb
20% less RAM after compaction 34gb vs 27gb
[No Churn](http://prombench.prometheus.io/grafana/d/7gmLoNDmz/prombench?orgId=1&var-RuleGroup=All&var-pr-number=6679&from=1588199791787&to=1588201716740)
20-30% less RAM -  23gb vs 18gb
40% less RAM after compaction 32.5gb vs 20gb

Screenshots are in [this comment](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/6679#issuecomment-621678932)

-----------------------

Prerequisite: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/6830 (Merged)

Closes https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/6377. More info in the linked issue _and_ the doc in that issue _and_ the doc inside that doc inside that issue :)


- [x] Add tests
- [x] Explore possible ways to get rid of new globals added in `head.go`
- [x] Wait for https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/6830 to be merged
- [x] Fix windows tests

@brian-brazil suggested a change to avoid iterating over the WAL twice during replay, and I am not sure why did that not hit me before :upside_down_face: 

Current replay:
1. Iterate over the WAL and only process the series records, hence loading all the empty series in memory.
2. Replay back the mmapped chunks and attach them to the relevant series.
3. Iterate the WAL again and replay the remaining samples.

New suggested change:
1. Replay the mmapped chunks and hold the map of series ID to the mmapped chunks in the memory.
2. Do the normal WAL replay as we have now, and whenever we come across a series record, attach the mmapped chunks from the map to that series.

I will make this change on Monday (or weekend) and run prombench again to test the replay. This is going to remove a lot of additional complexity brought by splitting up the WAL replay!

issue_context.title: Flush Head chunks to disk
issue_context.body:
The idea is to flush the head chunks to disk as soon as it is full and use it for the following purposes

1. mmap the flushed chunks in the Head instead of holding it in the memory, hence reducing the memory footprint of Head
2. Consider those chunks as checkpoints and process WAL accordingly, hence reducing the WAL replay time heavily

I had attempted checkpointing the chunks and replaying it [here](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/6059), but the idea has evolved since then (as described above).

I will come up with a design doc to comment on in the coming weeks.

/cc @brancz @krasi-georgiev

Edit: The high-level design doc https://docs.google.com/document/d/184urkLQnM7rqLmGvS66I15jU2pyPk_qwd8v_qDlXczo/edit?usp=sharing
comments: The completed chunks aren't sufficient as a checkpoint, you'd also need to checkpoint all non-completed chunks. You can then replay the WAL from only that checkpoint - after loading in all the completed chunks.

Yes, in my previous attempt I was writing all the chunks (complete and incomplete). But in this case (initial idea), where we write out the chunks in real-time when they are complete (and not like a checkpoint exactly), writing incomplete chunks would be rather expensive to mmap (but can be done only for the replay purpose). I will keep this in mind when working on the design doc, thanks!
And we'd still have the complete chunks via mmap hopefully, which would make them off-heap and save RAM.
I have jotted down some high-level ideas in this doc https://docs.google.com/document/d/184urkLQnM7rqLmGvS66I15jU2pyPk_qwd8v_qDlXczo/edit?usp=sharing

I was looking at the replay part of this work (work going on in this branch https://github.com/codesome/prometheus/tree/mmap-chunks) and I feel the need to change the format of samples record in Head (basically add another one).

If we are to decode the samples record and perform appends only to find out the all the samples are out of order after having the m-mapped chunks already restored, then it is going to be a lot of waste of time.

To take advantage of Head chunks on disk for replay speed, I wish to add uncompressed maxt to all samples record (max time among all the samples in that record), so that we can skip the record whose maxt is less than the smallest maxt among all the series currently loaded.

More ideas are welcome.

I have another idea. While we are flushing chunk to the disk whenever we complete a chunk, we can encode the segment number and the byte at which the WAL exists during flushing along with the chunk.

This way, when replaying the WAL, we can get the max WAL reference from all the series, and start replaying WAL from the min among them.

> This way, when replaying the WAL, we can get the max WAL reference from all the series, and start replaying WAL from the min among them.

Given churn, I'd expect this to require always doing everything.
Good point, didn't think about churn :(

I think the comments are confusing. Here we are garbage collecting the `c`, which is `*memChunk`, while the reader uses `c.chunk`. So setting c.chunk `nil` does not garbage collect `c.chunk` as it is referenced somewhere else already. Note that we are collecting `c` after `c.chunk` is already used somewhere.
Does that make sense?
hm , no sorry I didn't understand what you mean.

Here `c` and `c.chunk` are 2 different things (basically 2 pointers). After calling `s.chunk()`, we are mainly using `c.chunk`, so we should not garbage collect `c.chunk`. But the struct that is holding it, `c`, can be garbage collected (added back to the pool). Garbage collecting it does not affect `c.chunk`, and setting `c.chunk = nil` also does not affect `c.chunk` as that means changing the pointer and not the value inside the struct pointed by the pointer.

That is how our XOR chunks is designed as I see it https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/fd4521d2ebac6e467dd35db1e38c0e97aad49921/tsdb/chunkenc/xor.go#L77-L80

From another comment: I am planning to keep it m-map* for now and follow up later for this change, there are many places to make this change. I have `memory-map*` for metrics for now as that is end user-facing.

How is it guaranteed that the mmaped chunks are time sorted?

This slice works like the `chunks` slice just that they are mmapped. So the chunk gets appended to the back of the slice whenever a new chunk is cut, and that happens in the time sorted order. And mmapping happens in the same order, hence the replay of mmaping chunks are also in time sorted order. (Additionally, we check for out of order chunks when replaying mmapped chunks)
